message.content:
**Most Famous American Composers (by era)**  

| Era | Composer | Notable Works | Why They’re Famous |
|-----|----------|---------------|--------------------|
| **Early 19th – mid‑19th century** | **Stephen Foster** | “Oh! Susanna,” “Camptown Races” | Pioneered the “American folk‑song” style; his tunes became national standards. |
| | **John Philip Sousa** | “The Stars and Stripes Forever,” “Washington Post March” | King of the American march; his music defined U.S. patriotic and parade music. |
| **Late 19th – early 20th century** | **George Gershwin** | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris” | Blended jazz idioms with classical forms; helped legitimize jazz as concert music. |
| | **Aaron Copland** | “Appalachian Spring,” “Rodeo” | Created a distinctly “American” sound using open harmonies and folk motifs. |
| **Mid‑20th century** | **Leonard Bernstein** | “West Side Story,” “On the Town” | Broadway genius who also conducted the New York Philharmonic; bridged popular and classical worlds. |
| | **Philip Glass** | “Glassworks,” “Einstein on the Beach” | Minimalist pioneer; his repetitive structures reshaped contemporary classical music. |
| **Late 20th – 21st century** | **John Adams** | “Short Ride in a Fast Machine,” “Nixon in China” | Post‑minimalist composer whose works are widely performed worldwide. |
| | **Steve Reich** | “Music for 18 Musicians,” “Different Trains” | Minimalist innovator; his tape loops and phasing techniques are foundational. |
| | **John Williams** | Film scores for *Star Wars*, *Jaws*, *Indiana Jones* | One of the most recognizable film composers; his themes are iconic. |

These composers are frequently cited as the most influential and widely recognized figures in American music history.
